DCS Controller Loading: How to Calculate CPU and Memory Load and Keep Spare Capacity Within Limits

A controller that runs at 90 percent today has no room for tomorrow's loops, alarms or online downloads. Here we estimate CPU and memory load, pick execution periods and prove spare capacity before the plant starts up.

CPU load formula Solved example Execution periods FAT spare checks Free calculator

Every control module, I/O scan and display request takes a slice of controller time. Here we add those slices up, compare them with a loading limit and see what to change when the number is too high.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how to calculate DCS controller loading, why it matters for stable control, and how to keep enough spare capacity for future changes.
Quick Answer

How do you calculate DCS controller loading?

DCS controller loading is the share of each execution cycle the CPU spends on work, written as a percentage. Add, for each execution class, the module count times the time per module divided by the execution period, then add a fixed overhead. For example, 60 loops at 0.8 ms every 250 ms plus 240 modules at 0.5 ms every 1000 ms plus 15 % overhead gives 46.2 % load.

  1. List every control module with its execution period
  2. Estimate the execution time of each module from vendor data or a test
  3. Add module time divided by period for every class
  4. Add overhead for I/O scan, communication and redundancy
  5. Compare the total with the project loading limit and measure it again at FAT

What Is DCS Controller Loading?

DCS controller loading is the percentage of a controller's processing time and memory already used by its configured control modules, I/O scanning and communication. The rest is free time, the reserve that absorbs peaks, online changes and future loops.

Key Facts
  • Load per class = modules × time per module ÷ execution period
  • Fixed overhead covers I/O scan, communication and redundancy sync
  • ABB states 60 % total controller load as the ceiling for its optimised OPC subscription rules in System 800xA 5.1
  • Memory loading is checked separately from CPU loading

If you are new to the hardware itself, start with our overview of the distributed control system and how the engineering station, operator station and automation station share the work. Loading is the number that tells you how close the automation station is to its limit.

Do You Know?

A controller does not slow down gently when it runs out of time. When the work of one cycle cannot finish inside the period, modules start missing their scheduled execution, and loops behave as if they had a longer and irregular sample time.

What Consumes Controller Capacity?

Controller capacity is used by four things: executing control modules, scanning I/O cards, serving data to operator and engineering stations, and keeping a redundant partner in step. Only the first one is easy to see in your configuration, which is why loading estimates often come out too low.

Communication load grows with open displays, trends, historian tags and peer links. That is why DCS controller loading is often higher in the control room at shift change than on the test bench.

Control execution

PID, logic and sequence blocks. Cost depends on block type and period.

Best for: Most of the predictable load
Largest
I/O scan

Reading and writing the I/O cards.

Best for: Fixed per card and scan rate
Steady
Communications

Displays, alarms, historian collection and peer links.

Best for: Varies with operator activity
Variable
Redundancy sync

Keeping the standby controller in step for a bumpless switchover.

Best for: Redundant pairs only
Fixed
Quick Tip

When a vendor tool shows load per module, sort the list by cost. In most projects a small group of large modules, often with heavy calculation or many alarms, uses a big share of the time.

How to Calculate DCS Controller Loading

To calculate DCS controller loading, add the time every module needs per second of operation and express it as a percentage of one second, then add the overhead. Doing it per execution class keeps the arithmetic short.

Class load = n × t ÷ T
n = number of modules in the class
t = execution time per module (ms)
T = execution period (ms)
Total load = Σ class loads + overhead

Take the time per module from vendor performance data or a test controller, and keep t and T in the same unit.

1
Build the module list
Take it from the instrument I/O list, one line per loop, motor, valve and sequence.
2
Assign execution periods
Group modules by period, such as 250 ms, 500 ms and 1 s.
3
Estimate module cost
Use vendor figures or test results for typical PID, motor and valve templates.
4
Add the classes
Multiply count by time and divide by period for each class, then add them.
5
Add overhead
Include I/O scan, communication and redundancy sync as a stated assumption.

Solved Example of a Controller Load Calculation

A controller has 60 fast PID loops at 0.8 ms each running every 250 ms, 240 slower monitoring and logic modules at 0.5 ms each running every 1000 ms, and an assumed 15 % overhead. The total comes to 46.2 %, which leaves 13.8 % below a 60 % limit.

Fast class = 60 × 0.8 ÷ 250
= 0.192 = 19.2 %
Slow class = 240 × 0.5 ÷ 1000
= 0.12 = 12 %
Total = 19.2 + 12 + 15
= 46.2 %
Margin = 60 minus 46.2 = 13.8 %
Extra fast loops = 0.138 × 250 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 43

Now change only the execution period. Move those 60 loops from 250 ms to 500 ms and their share falls from 19.2 % to 9.6 %, so the total drops to 36.6 % without deleting a single module.

How to Choose the Execution Period for Control Modules

Choose the slowest execution period that still controls the process well, because every halving of the period doubles that module's share of the CPU. A common rule of thumb is to run a loop several times faster than the process responds, and no faster.

Module typeTypical period chosenReason
Fast flow and pressure loops250 to 500 msProcess responds in seconds
Level and temperature loops1 sSlow, large time constants
Motor and valve logic500 ms to 1 sInterlock reaction time
Monitoring and indication1 to 2 sNo control action
Totalisers and calculations1 to 5 sValue changes slowly

These are typical figures from project practice rather than vendor limits, so check them against your process and the control strategy for each unit. Loops that are part of override or selector control should run at the same period so the selected output does not jump between scans.

Do You Know?

Several controllers let you set a phase or offset for slow modules so they do not all start in the same base cycle. Spreading them out does not reduce the average load, but it flattens the peak that a single crowded cycle would show.

What Is Controller Free Time?

Controller free time is the share of the cycle left over after all scheduled work, so free time equals 100 % minus the load. Some systems show load and others show free time, and you need to know which one your diagnostics screen reports before you compare it with a limit.

The controller draws on free time during an online download, an alarm flood, a burst of display requests or a redundancy switchover. Those are exactly the moments when you most need control to stay steady.

Myth: A controller at 85 % load is fine because it still has 15 % left.
Fact: Average load hides peaks, and an online change or alarm flood can push a busy controller past 100 % for several cycles.
Myth: Load only depends on the number of loops.
Fact: Execution period, block type, alarm count and communication traffic matter as much as the loop count.

Spare Capacity at FAT and Typical Loading Limits

Spare capacity at FAT is proved by measuring peak controller load with the final configuration downloaded and the operator stations connected. Take the limit you compare against from the project specification and the vendor's own guidance.

SourceWhat it states
ABB System 800xA 5.1 System GuideController load should not exceed 60 % total load to use the optimised OPC subscription rules
ABB System 800xA 5.1 System GuidePublishes communication throughput figures measured at 40 % cyclic load
Zero Instrument spare capacity guide50 % or less at FAT or SAT, 60 % or less after commissioning, never above 70 %
Typical project specification practiceA separate spare figure for memory and for I/O, written into the FAT procedure

ABB ties its 60 % figure to the throughput and response of the connectivity server, so loading affects more than control execution. For other platforms, take the number from the vendor's sizing documents and write it into your specification before the factory acceptance test.

  • Final application downloaded, including all alarms and history tags
  • Operator stations connected with typical displays and trends open
  • Peak load recorded over a period long enough to include slow modules
  • Load recorded during an online download and a redundancy switchover
  • Memory usage recorded against the specified spare

How to Check DCS Controller Memory Loading

Memory loading is the used application memory divided by the memory available for applications, checked separately because a controller can be light on CPU and still short of memory. ABB's system guide, for example, treats memory size, available memory and execution performance as separate topics.

Memory grows with module count, history buffers, large arrays and every online change that keeps an old and a new version side by side for a moment. That last point matters if you plan to use online download in run mode, because the controller needs room for the new configuration before it can switch over.

Good ways to free capacity
  • Slow down monitoring modules that do no control
  • Move a group of loops to another controller in the same unit
  • Spread slow modules across phases or offsets
Habits that quietly overload
  • Running every module at the fastest period
  • Adding peer links instead of grouping related loops
  • Ignoring load after each online change
Quick Tip

Keep a simple loading log for each controller with the date, load, memory and the change that was made. A sudden jump after a small change points straight at the module to inspect.

Troubleshooting High DCS Controller Loading

Troubleshooting high DCS controller loading starts with finding whether the extra load comes from control execution, communication or a single module. Compare the present figures with the FAT baseline first, since that tells you what has changed.

SymptomLikely causeWhat to do
Load rose after a project changeNew modules at a fast periodReview periods of the new modules
Load high only at shift changeMany displays and trends openedCheck communication load and display design
Load spikes every few secondsSlow modules all in one cycleSpread them with phase or offset
Overruns reported on one moduleHeavy calculation or loop in logicSimplify or split the module

Communication load often comes from the network side, so check the control network layout and the protocols used for third party links when the load follows operator activity.

DCS Controller Loading FAQ

What is a safe CPU load for a DCS controller in operation?

A safe load is whatever your vendor and project specification state, and ABB, for example, uses 60 % total load as a ceiling for its OPC rules. Many end user specifications ask for a lower figure at FAT so the plant keeps room for later changes.

How do you calculate DCS controller loading step by step with an example?

Multiply module count by time per module, divide by the period, add the classes and add overhead. For 60 loops at 0.8 ms every 250 ms, 240 modules at 0.5 ms every 1000 ms and 15 % overhead, the total load is 46.2 %.

What is the difference between controller load and controller free time?

Load is the share of the cycle used by scheduled work, while free time is the share left over. They always add up to 100 %, so a controller showing 35 % free time is running at 65 % load.

Why does controller load go up when operators open more displays?

Every open display, trend and alarm list asks the controller for fresh data at its own update rate. That communication work runs on the same CPU as control, so DCS controller loading can rise at shift change even when nobody has changed the configuration.

How does execution period affect DCS controller CPU load?

The load of a module is inversely proportional to its period, so halving the period doubles its share. In the solved example, moving 60 loops from 250 ms to 500 ms cuts their share from 19.2 % to 9.6 %.

What is the most common mistake when checking controller loading at FAT?

The usual mistake is measuring with operator stations disconnected and only reading the average. Record the peak dcs controller loading with displays open, during an online download and during a redundancy switchover, then keep those figures as the FAT baseline.

What We Learn Today

  • DCS controller loading is the sum of each module class count times execution time divided by period, plus a fixed overhead for I/O and communication.
  • Execution period has the biggest effect on load, so choose the slowest period that still controls the process well and retune loops after changes.
  • Prove spare capacity at FAT by recording peak CPU and memory load with displays open, during online downloads and during redundancy switchover tests.
